User: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm married filing jointly in Boston MA. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $12,500 in 1099 income (IT contracting, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2016–2020). I donated $1,400 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $890 in work expenses. What can I deduct,

and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
Assistant: I can help — below is a clear summary of what you can likely deduct, whether you should itemize, what tax forms you’ll need, and a few questions so I can give a tighter estimate of tax owed.

Quick answer (likely): You will almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2023 (MFJ = $27,700). Your most useful deductions are (1) student loan interest (above-the-line, up to $2,500 if you qualify) and (2) business deduction

s for your 1099 contracting (home office and business expenses) which reduce your self-employment income and create a deduction for half your self-employment tax. The $1,400 charitable gift only helps if you itemize — since your likely itemized total is far below $27,700, itemizing won’t help unless you have other big deductions (mortgage interest, large state/local taxes, big medical expenses, etc.).

What you can deduct (and where)
- Student loan interest (above-the-line): Up to $2,500 (Form 1040 adjustme

nt), subject to MAGI phaseouts (for MFJ 2023 the phaseout begins at $145k). This reduces your AGI directly.
- Self-employment income deductions (Schedule C):
  - Home office (business use of home): You can use either the simplified method (140 sq ft × $5 = $700) or the actual method (business % × allowable home expenses). Your business percentage = 140 / 620 ≈ 22.58%. Annual rent = $2,400 × 12 = $28,800; business portion of rent ≈ $6,504. The actual method is much larger here, so it will generally be better

if the office is used exclusively and regularly for your contracting work.
  - Other business expenses: If your $890 in “work expenses” relate to your 1099 IT contracting (clients), those are deductible on Schedule C. If they are unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job, they are NOT deductible for 2018–2025.
- Self-employment tax: You will owe self-employment tax on net self-employment earnings (Schedule SE). You may deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1).
- Interest inco

me: The $1,450 (Marcus) + $320 (TD Ameritrade) = $1,770 interest is taxable. Because total interest > $1,500, you will file Schedule B to report interest.
- Charitable giving: $1,400 to St. Mary’s Food Bank is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). No special universal “above-the-line” deduction for cash gifts for 2023.

Other possible items
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: If your net self-employment income qualifies, you may be eligible for up to a 20% deduction of QBI (Form 8995). Wheth

er it applies and how much depends on your net profit after expenses and other limits.
- State & local taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses: you didn’t mention these; if you have significant amounts they could change the itemize vs standard decision.

Rough impact illustration (two contracting-expense scenarios)
(assumptions: your 1099 income = $12,500; W-2 = $64,800; interest = $1,770; student loan interest eligible and you claim max $2,500)

1) If your $890 expenses ARE business-related and yo

u use the actual home-office method:
- Home-office (actual): ≈ $6,504; + $890 other expenses = $7,394 total business expenses
- Net SE profit ≈ $12,500 − $7,394 = $5,106
- SE tax ≈ $720 (you deduct half ≈ $360 as adjustment)
- Student loan interest deduction (assume $2,500) reduces AGI
- Standard deduction ($27,700) is still far larger than your itemized charitable $1,400, so you would take the standard deduction.

2) If your $890 expenses are NOT business-related (employee expenses) and home office is NOT

for your contracting:
- You cannot deduct the $890 (suspended), and you cannot take home-office deductions for your W-2 work.
- You still claim student loan interest (up to $2,500) and report interest income.
- Standard deduction again almost certainly wins.

Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (individual return)
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments to Income) — student loan interest, half SE tax
- Schedule B — for interest income (total > $1,500)
- Schedule C — Profit or Loss from Business (for the 1099 contracti

ng)
- Schedule SE — Self-Employment Tax
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (ONLY if you use the actual method for home office)
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — Qualified Business Income Deduction (if applicable)
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (seems unlikely here unless you have other large itemizable amounts)

Actionable next steps / what I need to give you a precise estimate
1. Confirm whether the $890 in work expenses are business expenses related to the 1099 IT contracting (if y

es, they’re deductible on Schedule C; if no, they’re not deductible).
2. Confirm whether the $3,600 student loan interest is the amount paid in 2023 (if yes, the deductible amount will be capped at $2,500; if it’s a total outstanding interest or multi-year number, tell me the interest paid in 2023).
3. Tell me if you had any of the following in 2023: mortgage interest, property tax payments, large state income tax payments, unreimbursed medical expenses, retirement contributions (IRA / SEP / Solo 401k), or

estimated tax payments.
4. Tell me whether your home office is used exclusively for the 1099 contracting (you said “home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use)” — confirm it’s for your contracting work).

If you want, I can:
- Run a worked example with numbers (estimate taxable income, self-employment tax, and approximate federal tax) using either the actual or simplified home office method.
- Prepare a checklist of records and receipts to have when you (or your preparer) file.
- Draft an email to your tax prepa

rer with all of this info and the documents they’ll need.

Would you like me to run an estimated tax calculation? If so, confirm items 1–3 above (especially whether the $890 is for the 1099 work and how much student loan interest was paid in 2023).
